title: LG Energy Solution secures US lithium supply for ten years - electrive.com
content:
LG Energy Solution has signed a long-term supply agreement with Smackover Lithium. Starting in 2029, the battery manufacturer plans to source 8,000 tons of lithium carbonate from Arkansas annually as it scales US production of batteries for EVs and stationary storage.
LG Energy Solution secures long-term lithium carbonate from Arkansas.
Image: LG Energy Solution
The agreement covers a total of 80,000 tonnes of battery-grade lithium carbonate over a ten-year period. Deliveries are set to coincide with the start of commercial production at the South West Arkansas (SWA) Project in 2029. According to LG, the agreement is a binding take-or-pay contract, with prices and other commercial terms remaining confidential.
Smackover Lithium is a joint venture founded in 2024 by Standard Lithium and Equinor. Standard Lithium holds 55 per cent and acts as the operator, while Equinor owns 45 per cent. Together, the partners are developing multiple projects involving direct lithium extraction from brine in Arkansas and Texas. The South West Arkansas Project could achieve an annual production capacity of 22,500 tonnes of lithium carbonate in its first phase. With the agreed 8,000 tonnes per year, LG Energy Solution would take more than a third of the planned production.
LGES is already the second major customer for the project. In March, Smackover Lithium signed another
ten-year contract for 8,000 tonnes per year with commodity trader Trafigura
. Overall, the joint venture aims to secure long-term buyers for around 80 per cent of its planned production capacity. According to Smackover Lithium, the two existing contracts already cover around 90 per cent of this targeted offtake volume. Another, smaller contract is still to follow.
US lithium to strengthen local supply chain
The offtake agreements also play a key role in financing the project. According to Smackover Lithium, three export credit agencies have expressed interest in providing debt financing totalling more than one billion dollars. However, a final investment decision is still pending and is expected to be made later this year. Construction is then set to begin ahead of commercial production in 2029.
The lithium is to be extracted from brine using Direct Lithium Extraction (DLE) and then processed into battery-grade lithium carbonate. This method involves separating the lithium directly from the brine, rather than using large evaporation ponds. In its announcement, LGES highlights the sustainability benefits of the process, though the company does not quantify how these compare to other extraction methods.
For LG Energy Solution, the contract is key to localising its North American supply chain. The lithium carbonate produced in Arkansas is intended to meet the requirements for raw materials that do not originate from a so-called ‘prohibited foreign entity’. The Korean battery manufacturer now has an
extensive production network in the USA
. In its announcement, LGES particularly points to the strong growth of the North American market for stationary energy storage. The company is currently significantly expanding its US business with LFP cells for such applications. By the end of 2026, more than 50 GWh of production capacity for LFP cells for stationary storage is set to be established across three of its own sites and two partner-operated locations in North America.
In its new
plant in Lansing, Michigan
, LGES has recently started battery production. The facility produces LFP cells for stationary storage,
including for Tesla
. In the future, NMC cells for Toyota’s electric vehicles will also be manufactured in Lansing.

title: Future Challenges in the Battery Market: Building Circular Battery Systems Beyond Recycling - Batteries News
content:
Future Challenges in the Battery Market: Building Circular Battery Systems Beyond Recycling – Why Tomorrow’s Battery Value Chain Requires a System-Wide Approach
Battery demand is accelerating fast — lithium demand alone grew 30% in 2024 and could rise fivefold by 2040 — putting growing pressure on critical raw materials.
Recycling is essential, but on its own it can only address part of the challenge: real circularity depends on design, collection, EPR, logistics, traceability and reuse working together.
Collection remains the biggest bottleneck — the EU collects only ~45% of portable batteries today, well short of the 73% target for 2030.
New battery chemistries like LFP and sodium-ion demand more flexible, adaptable recycling systems rather than one-size-fits-all solutions.
There is no universal blueprint: effective circular systems must be adapted to local markets and infrastructure, as shown by projects like BATTPRO in Cambodia.
Long-term resilience depends on collaboration across the entire value chain — not on any single technology or regulation.
Introduction
The global battery market is entering a new era.
Driven by electrification, renewable energy integration and digitalisation, batteries have become one of the key enabling technologies of the 21st century. Electric vehicles, stationary energy storage systems and countless portable devices are accelerating demand at an unprecedented pace: Lithium demand alone grew by 30% in 2024 and is projected to increase fivefold by 2040, with graphite and nickel demand both doubling over the same period [
] [1]. This scale of growth is increasing pressure on the supply of critical raw materials while at the same time, new battery chemistries and evolving regulatory frameworks are fundamentally reshaping the industry.
This rapid transformation creates enormous opportunities. However, it also raises a fundamental question that extends far beyond battery production itself:
How can society ensure that tomorrow’s batteries become
tomorrow’s
resources?
For many years, the discussion has focused primarily on recycling technologies. And the potential is real: with efficient circularity, recycled materials could cover up to 25% of lithium demand by 2040, up to 50% of nickel demand, and more than 60% of cobalt demand in the EU [
] [2]. Yet recycling remains only one part of a much larger system. Efficient collection, extended producer responsibility (EPR), consumer participation, safe logistics, digital traceability, second-life applications and international collaboration are equally critical to creating truly circular battery value chains.
The transition towards a circular battery economy is therefore not simply a technological challenge. It is a systems challenge.
Building resilient and sustainable battery markets will require integrated solutions that connect every stage of the battery lifecycle—from product design and market placement to collection, reuse, recycling and the recovery of valuable raw materials for new battery production.
This article explores the key challenges that will shape the future of battery circularity and discusses why building effective circular battery systems requires a holistic, system-wide approach rather than focusing on recycling alone.
The Battery Revolution Is Changing the Entire Value Chain
The global battery industry is undergoing one of the most profound transformations in its history. What began with the rapid growth of portable consumer electronics has evolved into a strategic industrial sector that underpins electric mobility, renewable energy integration, digital infrastructure and future economic resilience.
Across the world, governments and industries are investing billions in battery manufacturing, while new gigafactories, energy storage projects and electrification strategies continue to accelerate market growth. Yet this growth remains highly concentrated: China alone accounts for well over half of global raw material processing for lithium and cobalt and nearly 85% of global battery cell production capacity, making it both the industry’s largest producer and its largest consumer. As European demand rises rapidly and domestic production capacity is set to expand, the need for a more independent, circular battery economy has become a strategic priority. Part of Europe’s response is the EU Battery Regulation: It introduces an entirely new regulatory framework, establishing ambitious requirements for sustainability, due diligence, recycled content, collection targets and digital product information.
This transformation is about much more than increasing battery production. It fundamentally changes how batteries must be designed, marketed, collected, reused and ultimately recycled. As battery technologies continue to evolve—from nickel-rich chemistries towards lithium iron phosphate (LFP), LMFP and future sodium-ion technologies—the entire circular value chain must evolve alongside them. Existing collection systems, recycling processes and economic models can no longer be assumed to meet tomorrow’s requirements.
Consequently, the battery industry faces a critical transition: while technological innovation has advanced at remarkable speed, the development of circular systems capable of managing future battery streams must now keep pace.
Circular Economy Begins Long Before Recycling
Public discussions often associate battery circularity almost exclusively with recycling technologies. While efficient recycling remains indispensable, it represents only the final stage of a much broader system.
A truly circular battery economy begins much earlier—at product design, continues through responsible market placement, efficient collection infrastructures, consumer participation, safe transport, transparent material flows and informed policy frameworks before batteries ever arrive at a recycling facility.
Every stage of this lifecycle directly influences the next. Batteries that are not returned through appropriate collection channels cannot contribute to resource recovery. Poorly designed collection systems reduce recycling efficiency. Missing consumer awareness leads to valuable materials being lost in residual waste streams. Inadequate logistics increase both safety risks and operational costs.
In other words, recycling performance is largely determined long before the recycling process itself begins.
This systems perspective lies at the heart of Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR). Rather than focusing solely on waste treatment, modern EPR frameworks seek to organise the entire end-of-life management process—from collection and financing to treatment and reporting—while creating incentives for continuous system improvement. Across Europe, Producer Responsibility Organisations (PROs) have become key actors in coordinating these activities on behalf of producers, although implementation models continue to differ considerably between countries.
New Battery Chemistries Require New Circular Strategies
Another major transformation is taking place within the batteries themselves.
For many years, recycling technologies and business models have largely been developed around nickel- and cobalt-rich lithium-ion batteries. Today, however, lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries—which are approximately 30% cheaper than NMC batteries—are rapidly gaining market share across electric vehicles and stationary energy storage applications [
] [3]. Forecasts indicate that LFP could account for around 50% of the European market, while sodium-ion batteries are emerging as an additional low-cost chemistry [
McKinsey
This evolution creates significant new opportunities—but also important challenges for circularity.
Different chemistries require different recycling approaches, generate different economic incentives and recover different combinations of valuable materials. Technologies designed around one battery chemistry cannot automatically be transferred to another. At the same time, the European Battery Regulation introduces minimum recycled-content requirements for new batteries, creating additional pressure to establish reliable recovery pathways for critical raw materials.
Future recycling systems must therefore become increasingly flexible, capable of processing a growing diversity of battery chemistries while maintaining high recovery efficiencies and ensuring economically viable operations.
This illustrates an important reality: circular economy strategies must evolve alongside battery technologies rather than react to them years later.
Why Collection Systems Will Determine Future Recycling Success
Of all these upstream stages, collection is the one that will most directly determine future recycling success. Even the most advanced recycling technologies cannot recover valuable materials from batteries that never enter formal collection systems yet today, only around 49% of portable batteries are collected across the EU, well short of the 73% target set by the EU Batteries Regulation for 2030 [
Eurostat
Closing this gap will become increasingly challenging as portable batteries grow in both volume and chemical diversity and are integrated into an ever-expanding range of consumer products. Their widespread distribution, compact size and varying chemistries make efficient collection considerably more difficult than for many other waste streams. At the same time, improper disposal increases environmental risks and contributes to fire hazards in waste collection and sorting facilities. While portable batteries represented a significant waste stream in the past, electric vehicles and stationary storage batteries will account for a far larger and rapidly growing share of the market – adding a new dimension of scale to future collection and recycling needs.
Successful collection systems therefore require much more than conveniently located return points. They rely on clear regulatory frameworks, effective Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) schemes, public awareness, safe logistics, reliable financing mechanisms and close cooperation between producers, retailers, municipalities and recycling operators.
These upstream processes directly determine the quality, quantity and safety of batteries entering recycling facilities. In this respect, collection systems should no longer be viewed simply as waste management infrastructure. They are strategic components of future resource security and circular value creation.
As battery volumes continue to increase worldwide, strengthening collection systems will become one of the most important investments in the future resilience of battery circularity.
Battery circularity has become a global challenge, yet there is no universal blueprint for building effective collection and recycling systems.
Across Europe, Extended Producer Responsibility has evolved over several decades into a structured framework in which producers assume responsibility for the end-of-life management of batteries through collective systems and clearly defined legal obligations. The new EU Battery Regulation further strengthens this approach by introducing ambitious collection targets, recycled-content requirements and additional sustainability obligations across the battery value chain.
However, conditions differ significantly outside Europe. In Cambodia, for example, public collection structures for waste batteries are largely absent, meaning that only a fraction of batteries reaches appropriate treatment or recycling facilities. Informal collection and recycling activities continue to play a major role. Rather than transferring existing European models without adaptation, successful implementation requires solutions that reflect local market structures, regulatory environments and stakeholder landscapes.
This understanding forms the basis of the BATTPRO (Battery Takeback Professionalization to Support Environmental Protection in Cambodia and Thailand) project. Implemented by Stiftung GRS Batterien together with ECOLOGICON and supported by the German Federal Ministry for the Environment, Climate Action, Nature Conservation and Nuclear Safety (BMUKN/BMUV), the initiative seeks to strengthen sustainable battery take-back and recycling systems through international knowledge exchange and practical capacity building.
Based on analyses of local battery markets, collection structures and stakeholders, BATTPRO follows a phased approach that begins with pilot projects and the joint development of locally adapted solutions. Through coordinated action by consumers, producers, public authorities, logistics providers and recyclers, these pilots are intended to support the gradual establishment of EPR, collection, logistics and recycling structures, ultimately achieving nationwide coverage within ten years.
The same philosophy is reflected in international knowledge-sharing initiatives such as the “From Waste to Value” webinar and the Sardinia 2025 workshop, both of which emphasise that successful circular economy strategies are built through cooperation rather than replication. International experience provides valuable guidance, but effective implementation always requires adaptation to local realities.
Ultimately, global battery circularity will depend not only on technological innovation, but also on the ability to exchange knowledge across borders while respecting regional differences in infrastructure, regulation and market maturity.
Building Resilient Circular Battery Systems Through Collaboration
No single organisation can establish a circular battery economy alone.
Future battery systems will require coordinated action across the entire value chain, bringing together manufacturers, Producer Responsibility Organisations, recyclers, policymakers, researchers, logistics providers, retailers and consumers. Each stakeholder contributes to the performance of the overall system, and weaknesses at any stage inevitably affect the effectiveness of the whole.
This systems perspective becomes increasingly important as battery technologies continue to evolve and regulatory requirements become more ambitious. The introduction of recycled-content targets, digital product information and stricter sustainability criteria will require unprecedented levels of transparency and coordination across industries. The battery passport is a practical example of how this transparency can be achieved. By making relevant information on battery chemistry, material composition and performance available across the value chain, it can improve cooperation between stakeholders and enable safer, more efficient sorting and recycling processes.
Producer Responsibility Organisations occupy a unique position within this ecosystem. By coordinating collection, supporting regulatory compliance and facilitating cooperation between multiple stakeholders, they help translate legislative objectives into practical implementation. At the same time, research institutions and international partnerships contribute the scientific knowledge and innovation needed to continuously improve circular systems.
The growing complexity of future battery value chains therefore reinforces one central insight: resilience is created not by individual technologies, but by well-designed systems that connect all participants through shared objectives, clear responsibilities and continuous knowledge exchange.
Collaboration is no longer an optional complement to technological progress—it has become one of its essential preconditions.
Conclusion – The Future Depends on Systems, Not Individual Technologies
The transition towards battery-powered societies is accelerating across the globe. Electrification, renewable energy integration and digitalisation will continue to increase demand for batteries while simultaneously raising expectations for sustainability, resource efficiency and circularity.
Meeting these expectations requires a shift in perspective.
The future of battery circularity will not be determined by recycling technologies alone. It will depend on the strength of the systems connecting every stage of the battery lifecycle—from product design and market placement to collection, logistics, reuse, recycling and the reintegration of recovered materials into new battery production.
Circular economy is therefore not a single technology, nor a single regulation. It is a coordinated system of responsibilities, infrastructure, innovation and collaboration.
Building resilient battery value chains will require governments, industry, Producer Responsibility Organisations, research institutions and consumers to work together in ways that extend beyond traditional sector boundaries. International cooperation, knowledge exchange and locally adapted implementation strategies will become increasingly important as battery markets continue to expand worldwide.
The transformation towards a circular battery economy has already begun.
Its long-term success, however, will ultimately depend not on how efficiently we recycle batteries—but on how effectively we build the systems that make circularity possible in the first place.

title: Lead Intelligent Redefines Large-Scale Energy Storage Battery Manufacturing with Its Integrated Assembly Line Solution - Batteries News

Lead Intelligent Redefines Large-Scale Energy Storage Battery Manufacturing with Its Integrated Assembly Line Solution
As the global energy storage industry accelerates toward the TWh era, the rapid adoption of 500 Ah+ and even 1000 Ah+ large-format energy storage cells is reshaping the competitive landscape.
While larger cell formats deliver higher energy density and lower system costs, they also introduce significantly greater manufacturing challenges—from heavy-duty material handling and high-precision positioning to welding consistency and hermetic sealing. Conventional production lines, built around stand-alone equipment and incremental process optimization, are increasingly unable to balance productivity, yield, and cost, let alone meet the stringent requirements for stability, consistency, and manufacturing flexibility in large-scale production.
Built on 100% proprietary technologies and extensive experience in turnkey production line delivery, Lead Intelligent has launched its Integrated Assembly Line Solution for Large-Format Energy Storage Batteries. By deeply integrating manufacturing processes, intelligent equipment, logistics systems, and digital technologies, the solution establishes a new benchmark for efficiency, quality, and scalable production.
Simplifying the Production Line, Maximizing Manufacturing Efficiency
Moving beyond the fragmented layout of conventional production lines, Lead Intelligent adopts an integrated process architecture that consolidates multiple manufacturing operations into a unified production system. By reengineering the entire production workflow—from factory layout and material flow to operational management—the solution unlocks substantial gains in efficiency and productivity.
Optimized Factory Footprint and Asset Utilization
The integrated line reduces production floor space by 20% while decreasing the number of equipment units by 20%, maximizing factory utilization and significantly lowering capital investment.
Safer and More Efficient Material Flow
Lifecycle Operational Efficiency
Combined with intelligent power management and predictive maintenance systems, the solution reduces energy consumption and minimizes unplanned downtime, extending productivity gains across the entire lifecycle of the production line.
Core Technologies Delivering High-Quality Manufacturing
The Integrated Assembly Line Solution covers the complete manufacturing process for large-format energy storage batteries, including hot pressing, tab folding inspection, X-ray alignment inspection, X-ray foreign object detection, cell pairing, ultrasonic welding, laser welding, and helium leak testing.
Designed in accordance with automotive-grade manufacturing standards, the production line achieves cleanliness levels of up to ISO Class 5 at critical process stations, providing a highly controlled manufacturing environment for stable, high-volume production.
Drawing on years of expertise in lithium-ion battery manufacturing, Lead Intelligent continues to advance core process technologies to address the key challenges associated with assembling next-generation large-format energy storage cells.
High-Power Ultrasonic Welding Technology
The solution enables single-pass formation of extra-large welds, meeting the high-current requirements of multi-layer electrode tabs while eliminating the tab tearing risks commonly associated with secondary welding overlap.
Anti-Tab Tearing Process
Applied across ultrasonic welding, taping, and cell folding, this proprietary technology effectively resolves one of the industry’s most persistent challenges—tab tearing in large-format energy storage cells.
High-Precision Tab Forming Technology
Optimized Lid-to-Can Welding Solution
Enhanced weld-spatter extraction and improved welding reference consistency enable outstanding process stability, achieving a first-pass welding yield of at least 99.5% and a final production yield exceeding 99.9%.
End-to-End Collaboration That Delivers Scalable Manufacturing
Built on a unified process architecture, standardized interfaces, and an integrated data framework, Lead Intelligent seamlessly connects production equipment, intelligent logistics, MES, and quality management systems into a fully coordinated manufacturing ecosystem. The result is an end-to-end solution that supports customers throughout the entire production lifecycle—from commissioning to stable mass production.
Complete Process Visibility
Real-time synchronization of process parameters and full production traceability ensure stable manufacturing performance. The integrated production line achieves an Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) of over 80% while delivering an overall production yield exceeding 99%.
Flexible Compatibility Across Cell Formats
The solution supports rapid changeovers for the full range of 300 Ah+ to 1000 Ah+ large-format battery cells, enabling manufacturers to respond efficiently to current production requirements while providing the flexibility to accommodate future cell technology upgrades.
Proven Large-Scale Delivery Capability
Backed by more than 600 GWh of cumulative energy storage production line orders, Lead Intelligent has maintained the industry’s leading shipment volume for prismatic large-format energy storage battery production lines. Its proven expertise in large-scale turnkey delivery and global project execution provides customers with a reliable foundation for long-term manufacturing success.
Moving beyond optimizing individual machines to optimizing the entire production line is becoming essential as the energy storage industry enters the TWh era. End-to-end manufacturing integration is not only the key to reducing production costs and improving operational efficiency, but also a critical enabler of high-quality, sustainable industrial growth.
Looking ahead, Lead Intelligent will continue to leverage its fully proprietary technology portfolio, comprehensive turnkey delivery capabilities, and lifecycle service network to help customers accelerate capacity deployment and technology upgrades worldwide. Together with partners across the industry, the company is committed to building a safer, more efficient, and lower-carbon manufacturing ecosystem that supports the transition toward a net-zero energy future.

The Next Phase of LiFePO4 Battery Competition: From Specs to Full-Lifecycle Responsibility
LiTime’s Approach to R&D, Manufacturing, and Customer Support
How the market evaluates energy products is changing. Capacity, output and cycle life remain important, but as lithium ion batteries become embedded in long-term applications—from RVs and boats to off-grid systems and industrial equipment—customers are placing greater emphasis on robust product development, consistent manufacturing quality, responsive after-sales support and effective product-liability management.
is expanding its Full-Lifecycle Responsibility Framework to address these expectations. The company says the framework integrates reliability management across product development, manufacturing, customer support and product-risk management, with the goal of moving beyond supplying energy hardware to delivering long-term value.
Building reliability into development
For lithium ion batteries used in demanding, long-duration applications, reliability begins well before production starts.
LiTime incorporates product requirements, manufacturing feasibility and risk management into product planning, design validation, production launch and ongoing improvement. Its development process uses Advanced Product Quality Planning (APQP) to identify and manage potential design and manufacturing risks before mass production.
During product and process design, the company applies Failure Mode and Effects Analysis (FMEA) to identify potential failure points and define corrective measures. At the production-release stage, Production Part Approval Process (PPAP) methods are used to evaluate technical specifications, process flows, control plans and process capability, providing data-based support for mass-production readiness.
Standardized manufacturing and traceability
The long-term reliability of lithium batteries also depends on maintaining consistency and traceability in assembly, inspection and quality control throughout the battery manufacturing process.
LiTime applies standardized procedures and role-specific SOPs across incoming-material inspection, key-process controls, in-process inspection, final testing and shipment inspection. The company also records batch information and key production-process data, supporting traceability and corrective-action processes when quality issues occur.
According to LiTime’s internal quality-management data for 2026, standardized products included in its reporting achieved a final pass yield (FPY) of 99.75%.
The company also manages product compliance according to product category, target market and applicable regulations. To date, relevant LiTime products have obtained more than 380 certifications. Depending on the product and market, requirements may include UN38.3 transportation testing, CE-related compliance, RoHS restrictions and applicable FCC requirements.
Customer Support beyond delivery
For users, support needs often continue well beyond the purchase itself. Installation guidance, product-use education, troubleshooting and long-term maintenance can all shape the ownership experience.
LiTime offers warranties of up to five years and a 30-day return policy for eligible products, subject to local sales terms, warranty policies and applicable law. The company supports customers through its headquarters experience center, overseas local support teams and AI-enabled service tools, with multilingual assistance available across regions.
LiTime has also introduced a VIP service program that begins at the point of order. The program includes logistics-status notifications and exception alerts, installation guidance and post-sales follow-up, extending support across fulfillment, installation and ongoing use.
AIG agreement strengthens liability coverage
Product-risk management is increasingly important for energy brands serving global markets and long-term applications.
As part of its full-lifecycle responsibility strategy, LiTime has entered into a commercial general liability insurance agreement with American International Group (AIG) for its products. Within the scope of the policy, the coverage is intended to support a more efficient, professional and traceable response to relevant liability events.
The company says the arrangement further strengthens its long-term responsibility framework and provides additional confidence for customers using its products over extended periods.
Consistent performance remains central to battery ownership. But for batteries deployed in RVs, marine vessels, off-grid energy systems and industrial applications, long-term user experience also depends on how products are designed, manufactured, supported and managed after delivery.
Robert Li
, Chief Quality Officer of LiTime
Full-lifecycle responsibility means integrating risk prevention into the product-development stage and extending that responsibility throughout the customer’s ownership experience.
“By continuously strengthening responsibility management across every stage, LiTime aims to go beyond product delivery and provide users and partners with support throughout the product lifecycle—building long-term trust through ongoing service.”

title: AI is Driving the Future of Battery Supply Chains
content:
Battery Manufacturing

Aclara Resources and Argonne National Laboratory leverage advanced modeling and digital twins to enhance manufacturing processes for next-generation battery materials.
August 31, 2026
6 Min Read
AI and critical materials shaping future battery supply chains.
AI illustration generated for Battery Technology.
As global demand for more efficient and affordable batteries continues to grow, the conversation is expanding beyond battery chemistry alone. Successfully serving those markets at scale also depends on something equally important: resilient, domestic supply chains for the
critical materials
needed by the industries and technologies that rely on advanced batteries.
Manufacturing products powered by advanced batteries – including industrial equipment, defense systems, consumer electronics and transportation technologies – requires not only traditional battery materials but also a broader portfolio of relatively low-volume yet strategically important materials, including rare earth elements.
As a result, developing the next generation of energy storage technologies is no longer just about battery performance. It also requires a deeper understanding of how the availability and production of critical materials influence the broader supply chains and downstream technologies they support.
Related:
LG Energy Solution North America President on Battery Market Pivot
A new collaboration between rare earth mineral company
Aclara Resources
and the U.S. Department of Energy’s
Argonne National Laboratory
highlights how artificial intelligence, advanced process modeling and public-private partnerships can help address that challenge.
Looking beyond discovery to deployment
For decades, battery innovation has focused on developing better materials with higher energy density, longer lifetimes and improved safety. Today, however, many of the industry’s greatest opportunities lie in commercialization.
How can promising laboratory discoveries be manufactured consistently at industrial scale? How can complex chemical processes be optimized before companies invest hundreds of millions of dollars in production facilities? And how can manufacturers reduce technical risk while accelerating time to market?
Answering those questions is driving growing interest in digital engineering tools that combine scientific understanding with operational data.
Among the most promising are AI-enabled digital twins – virtual representations of manufacturing processes that allow engineers to simulate, analyze, and optimize operations before making changes in the physical world.
A case study in critical materials
Aclara and Argonne are applying that approach to one of the most technically challenging areas of critical materials processing: heavy rare earth separation.
Through an R&D agreement, the partners are developing an AI-enabled digital twin of Aclara’s separation process using data generated at the company’s pilot facility, which was developed in collaboration with Virginia Tech University.
Related:
Inside LGES's New $2B Michigan Battery Plant
Argonne brings expertise in artificial intelligence, advanced computing, process modeling, and solvent extraction science. Together, those capabilities will be used to model the behavior of Aclara’s separation process under a wide range of feedstock compositions, allowing engineers to evaluate potential improvements virtually before implementing them at commercial scale.
Those insights will support Aclara's planned $277 million, first-of-its-kind heavy rare earth separation facility in Louisiana, which is expected to begin production by mid-2028. The facility will process feedstock from the company's ionic clay deposits into separated heavy rare earth oxides, including dysprosium, terbium, and yttrium, helping to strengthen the domestic supply chain for these strategically important materials.
For Aclara, the collaboration is intended to improve process performance, reduce the technical uncertainty that accompanies scaling a sophisticated separation process from pilot operations to commercial production, and ultimately help accelerate deployment of domestic critical materials production.
“This partnership with Argonne is a critical accelerator for Aclara’s strategy to establish a reliable US-based supply chain for heavy rare earths,” stated Ramón Barúa, CEO of Aclara Resources. “By combining our proprietary separation technology and pilot-scale data with Argonne's world-class capabilities in advanced computing, we are significantly reducing scale-up risk, accelerating industrial deployment and strengthening the foundations of a secure domestic supply of these critical minerals.”
Related:
Anthro Energy Breaks Ground on US Facility
Why battery manufacturers should care
At first glance, heavy rare earth separation may seem only indirectly related to batteries. After all, dysprosium and terbium are not active materials in today’s lithium-ion battery cells.
Yet they are essential components of high-performance permanent magnets used in many electric motors that power battery-electric and hybrid vehicles, as well as numerous industrial, defense and clean energy technologies.
More broadly, the collaboration illustrates an important reality for the battery industry: resilient downstream supply chains depend on a much larger critical materials ecosystem.
Manufacturers increasingly recognize that bottlenecks affecting any strategically important material – not just those inside a battery cell – can slow product adoption, increase costs and complicate long-term research and development.
Strengthening domestic processing capabilities across that ecosystem helps create more use case opportunities for advanced battery technologies.
Aclara has indicated that its planned Louisiana facility could ultimately supply more than 75% of US demand for dysprosium and terbium needed for electric vehicles (EVs), reducing dependence on overseas processing while supporting a growing domestic manufacturing base.
Picture:  Aclara’s Separation Pilot Plant at Virginia Tech, US. Courtesy of Aclara.
The bigger opportunity: Smarter manufacturing
Beyond the immediate rare earth application, the collaboration offers a glimpse into how AI could reshape manufacturing throughout the battery industry.
Many of the challenges confronting battery supply chains share common characteristics. Whether refining lithium, producing cathode precursor materials, separating nickel and cobalt, or recovering valuable elements from recycled battery black mass, manufacturers must optimize complex chemical processes while maintaining product quality, controlling costs, and scaling production efficiently.
Historically, much of that optimization has relied on iterative physical testing – a process that can consume considerable time and resources. Digital twins offer a different approach.
As additional operating data become available, the models continue improving, creating a feedback loop that supports continuous optimization throughout the life of a manufacturing facility.
While the production methodology being developed through the Aclara-Argonne collaboration is unique, digital twins have potential applications across a wide range of battery-material manufacturing and recycling processes.
Accelerating commercialization through partnership
The collaboration also demonstrates the complementary roles that industry and national laboratories play in strengthening US manufacturing.
Companies bring commercial insights, operational experience and real-world production challenges. National laboratories contribute multidisciplinary scientific expertise, advanced computing resources and specialized research capabilities that can help solve problems that extend beyond the scope of a single organization.
Together, those strengths can help bridge one of manufacturing’s most difficult transitions: moving innovative technologies from successful pilot operations to dependable commercial production.
“By combining real-world industry needs with deep expertise in the science of scale-up at national laboratories, we can speed the deployment of advanced technologies that strengthen domestic supply chains,” stated Claus Daniel, associate laboratory director for Argonne’s Advanced Energy Technologies directorate. “This work reflects Argonne's role in building regional industrial innovation hubs, such as the Gulf Coast and the Midwest, and leveraging complementary research capabilities to support U.S. competitiveness.”
For the battery industry, the science of scaling production through innovations in manufacturing, process engineering and critical materials production is becoming increasingly important as demand continues to grow.
Projects like the Aclara-Argonne collaboration demonstrate that artificial intelligence can contribute significantly. By combining advanced modeling with industrial expertise, the partnership helps build the manufacturing capabilities and resilient supply chains that will support the success of battery technology.

title: Volvo's cheapest EV can now power a campsite or coffee maker
content:
Volvo EX30
Peter Johnson
| Sep 1 2026 - 8:51 am PT
Volvo launched a software update that gives
the EX30
new capabilities, including the ability to power external electronics with vehicle-to-load (V2L).
Volvo EX30 gains V2L and more in latest update
Starting this week, EX30 drivers will be able to use their vehicle for more than just getting from point A to point B.
Volvo Cars is rolling out its latest over-the-air software update, giving the EX30 the ability to be used as a power bank on wheels.
With bidirectional charging, including vehicle-to-load (V2L), the EX30 can power external devices, such as a laptop, coffee maker, the fridge if the power goes out, or even a campsite using energy from the vehicle’s battery.
Delivering up to 3 kW at 16 amps, Volvo said the system can power “a wide range of everyday equipment.” It can be used when needed, but once the battery level drops below 20%, the system will automatically cut off the energy supply to save energy.
Volvo EX30 gains new features via OTA update (Source: Volvo Cars)
How does it work? With a separate adapter, you can connect it to the charge port and then plug in the device to draw power from the vehicle’s battery.
The V2L functions will not be available for EX30 drivers in the US, Canada, Mexico, Korea, Taiwan, or Japan. In the EMEA, APAC, and Latin America markets, it will use the CCS2 charging standard.
Volvo EX30 gains new features via OTA update (Source: Volvo Cars)
Volvo’s latest update also introduces a new user experience with a customizable contextual bar and redesigned settings menu.
In certain European markets, Volvo is introducing Plug & Charge capabilities for EX30 drivers. The ability streamlines public charging and eliminates the need for a physical card or extra app. It will only be available on 2026 models or newer.
Electrek’s Take
Adding bidirectional charging and V2L is a big update for the EX30, a feature that should already be offered on all EVs.
While it is disappointing to see those in the US will miss out, it’s not much of a surprise given Volvo announced it was
discontinuing the EX30
in the US after the 2026 model year.
Other entry-level electric vehicles, like the
2027 Kia EV3
, will fill the void left by the EX30. The 2027 Kia EV3 starts at $30,000, offers up to 321 miles of range, and comes with standard V2L.

title: Waymo opens robotaxi rides to the public in 3 new cities, now 14 total
content:
Fred Lambert
| Sep 1 2026 - 8:22 am PT
Waymo opened its driverless ride-hailing service to the general public in Denver, San Diego, and Tampa on Monday, bringing the Alphabet-owned company to 14 US cities.
Tens of thousands of people in each market had already signed up before the doors opened, and Waymo says it will let them in gradually over the coming weeks.
This isn’t the first time these three cities have shown up in a Waymo announcement. We reported in July that Waymo had
flipped Las Vegas to fully driverless and lined up Denver, San Diego, and Tampa as the next markets
. Back then, the service was still limited to employees and invited guests.
Now anyone can hail a ride. Riders in Denver and San Diego are getting Waymo’s new Zeekr-built vehicle, the roomier minivan-style platform running the company’s next-generation Waymo Driver, while the fleet fills out over the coming months.
Waymo has launched commercial service in seven new cities since March 2025, and it’s doing all of this while pushing toward a stated goal of 1 million paid rides a week by the end of the year. In May, the company
expanded its coverage area by more than 20% to over 1,400 square miles
, and in August it
won California approval to operate across 18 counties
The company leaned on its safety record for the rollout, saying its vehicles have been involved in 94% fewer serious-injury crashes than human drivers over the miles it has driven. To be fair, Waymo’s service mainly operates in lower-speed areas.
“From coast to coast, we’re focused on making everyday transportation safer, easier, and more accessible,” said Suzanne Philion, Waymo’s chief marketing officer.
Local officials showed up for the launch. Colorado Governor Jared Polis tied it to air quality, saying “Waymo’s launch helps us achieve cleaner air sooner,” and Tampa Mayor Jane Castor called it “another effective – and exciting – way to get around.” Waymo also worked with AARP Florida and the San Diego chapter of the National Federation of the Blind on accessibility ahead of the launch.
Tampa is where it gets interesting
One of these three cities isn’t like the others. Tampa is now a market where Waymo and Tesla are both running paid, “driverless” ride services at the same time.
added Tampa and Orlando to its Robotaxi service in July
, but the comparison isn’t close. Tesla’s active fleet is extremely limited, and its own Q2 chart
showed the service’s growth going flat
even as the company insisted it was expanding. Waymo is showing up in the same city with no one in the driver’s seat and tens of thousands of people already on the list.
Electrek’s Take
It does feel like Waymo is seriously scaling now. Adding three metros at once, with tens of thousands pre-signed in each, and now 14 cities total. Waymo isn’t running a pilot anymore. It’s running a business, and it’s compounding.
The Tampa overlap is the clearest scoreboard we’ve had. Tesla has spent two years promising that its camera-only approach would let it scale robotaxis faster and cheaper than anyone. Instead, it’s the one still babysitting a couple dozen cars with remote monitoring, while Waymo drops a fully driverless, public service into the same Florida market and moves on to the next one. The gap isn’t closing. It’s widening.
None of this means Waymo has won. The Zeekr-built vehicle needs to prove it can be produced at the volume a million weekly rides demands, and the unit economics of a hardware-heavy sensor stack across a growing but still limited market are still an open question.

title: Tesla confirms Full Self-Driving was active in a crash that killed a mother of five
content:
Fred Lambert
| Sep 1 2026 - 7:52 am PT
A Tesla Model Y turning left at an intersection collided with a pickup truck in Batavia, Illinois, killing a passenger in the Tesla — Maggie Espinosa, 37, a teacher and mother of five. It was reported as an ordinary intersection crash.
But Electrek was able to confirm that Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says the car’s driver-assist system was engaged as it made that turn. This is part of an
ongoing Electrek investigation
matching reported crashes to Tesla’s redacted NHTSA data.
What happened at Randall and McKee
Around 4:19 p.m. on March 25, 2026, a Tesla Model Y heading south on Randall Road tried to turn left onto McKee Street and struck a Dodge pickup traveling straight in the opposite direction, according to Batavia police. A Nissan SUV was also caught up in the crash.
Espinosa, a front-seat passenger in the Tesla, died of her injuries. A former kindergarten teacher, she left behind five children, including 2-year-old twins; a
GoFundMe for the family
raised more than $100,000. The Tesla’s driver and two others were injured.
What Tesla told the federal government
Under a NHTSA Standing General Order, automakers must report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact. Tesla filed a report on this crash — and it’s revealing.
Tesla marks the automation “Engagement Status” as
“Verified Engaged,”
and lists the 2026 Model Y’s pre-crash movement as
“Making Left Turn”
at 24 mph, at an intersection. It says the Tesla struck the front of the pickup, which had the right of way going straight. And it confirms Tesla holds the
event-data recorder, telematics, and video
of the crash.
Then it redacts the parts that would explain it: the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was within the system’s approved operating area — all as “confidential business information.”
We’ve laid out the complete record below — everything Tesla disclosed, and everything it blacked out.
Electrek
contacted Batavia PD to let them know that Tesla confirmed its ADAS was active during the crash and ask for an update on the investigation. Batavia PD said that the crash “remains under investigation and is currently under review by the Kane County State’s Attorney’s Office.” No charges have been filed. And in the public account, there was no mention of Autopilot, “Full Self-Driving,” or any driver-assist system.
Tesla Full Self-Driving vs Autopilot
This one points more directly at “Full Self-Driving” than the highway cases we’ve covered. An
unprotected left turn across oncoming traffic at an intersection
is a City-Streets maneuver — something FSD does, and something basic Autopilot cannot. Basic Autopilot is a highway lane-keeping system; it does not turn a car left onto a cross street. So a driver-assist car that was
verified engaged while making a left turn
was, in all likelihood, running FSD.
However, that doesn’t mean FSD was at fault in the crash, but we don’t know without all the data, and Tesla is the one gatekeeping it. It didn’t even want the public to know that FSD was active in the crash until we were able to connect the NHTSA report to the media and police reports about the crash.
How we matched it:
the NHTSA record is unredacted on location (Batavia), vehicle (2026 Model Y), the left-turn-into-a-pickup mechanics, the fatality, and the month — a combination unique to this crash. One caveat: the incident time Tesla logged (12:54 UTC) does not cleanly convert to the ~4:19 p.m. local time police reported, unlike the other crashes we’ve matched, so we’re flagging that discrepancy rather than relying on it; every other identifying detail lines up.
Electrek’s Take
A teacher and mother of five is dead, a county prosecutor is weighing whether anyone should be charged, and the single piece of evidence that would show what actually happened in that intersection, did the software make the turn, or the driver?, is sitting in Tesla’s servers.
Tesla is testing software it calls ‘beta’ on public roads, turning every road user into an unwilling lab rat. At the minimum, and really, that’s all we are advocating for here, is to get all the details about what happens when it goes wrong.
We know Tesla is quick to release data and massage it when it looks good for the company, but it hides everything else.
If you are going to market the product as “self-driving” and encourage users to “use their phones”, you can’t hide the data when the system is involved in a fatal crash.

title: In Sept, Tesla will re-launch 3 products it launched a decade ago, for a stock pump
content:
Tesla has a packed September ahead of it, with two confirmed and one rumored product launches. For a company that has gone so long without new products, it would be a big month… if all three of those products hadn’t been launched years ago already.
It’s September 2026, and we’ve got a lot to look forward to in the EV space.
First up, we’re finally going to see the launch of the Tesla Cybercab this Thursday, September 3. The Cybercab is a small, two-seat vehicle intended to be used fully autonomously as a robotaxi, and doesn’t even have a steering wheel or pedals, as it’s meant to operate without a driver at all times.
Second, Tesla has confirmed that late this month it will roll out the Tesla Semi, a fully-electric heavy duty semi truck. This promises to make goods delivery more efficient, which is important given that larger vehicles are responsible for well more than their fair share of the pollution that harms human health. There are other electric semis, but Tesla claims to offer a better value proposition than the rest of them.
Finally, there’s the specter of the next-gen Tesla Roadster. While nothing is announced yet, Tesla designer Franz von Holzhausen said the Roadster is coming “very soon,” and we have heard some rumors suggesting the month of September. The Tesla Roadster is meant to be a fully electric hypercar with bonkers performance specs, which CEO Elon Musk has said will be the “last best driver’s car” but also says that it will be able to “fly” (which doesn’t make sense).
It would be an exciting month… if we hadn’t been hearing about all of these products for years now.
Cybercab unveiled in 2024, but the idea is much older
The Cybercab is the newest of the three, having been originally revealed in 2024. That’s an acceptable time between reveal and production, if actually even a little quick (well, as long as we’re not comparing to China’s EV timelines).
But that ignores the years of robotaxi-related talk from Musk, who originally suggested way back in 2016 that Tesla owners who purchased FSD (software which the company sold for as much as $15,000 and still has not delivered) would be able to send their cars out as autonomous taxis to make them money.
At the time, this was meant to apply to Tesla’s consumer vehicles, and Tesla called the concept “Tesla Network.” Now, it’s branding it as “Robotaxi,” and Tesla has sent out its own vehicles to make money using FSD, but still won’t let you do it, despite that it sold software on the promise that you could (and that this software would turn cars into an “appreciating asset” due to gradual technological unlocks).
Tesla even cancelled the planned Model 2, an affordable consumer vehicle, to make room for the stripped-down Cybercab, which we have no indication will be purchaseable by consumers.
And don’t forget: Tesla has not solved self-driving. Neither the consumer-available FSD nor the Robotaxi-exclusive version that allows operation without someone in the driver’s seat is truly capable of unattended operation at all times, or even in more than a few geofenced areas. Releasing a car with no steering wheel makes no sense before you solve that problem.
So while we’ll soon see the Cybercab in some sort of action, it is based on a concept that is more than a decade late, it still doesn’t deliver on its promises, and Tesla turned it from something that would be publicly-available and that people spent tens of thousands of dollars on into something that Tesla alone can operate and potentially profit on, while consumers are restricted from doing the thing they were promised when they bought their product.
Tesla Semi was first shown in 2017, almost a decade ago
The Tesla Semi does stand to revolutionize trucking – or at least, it did 9 years ago when it was first shown with a planned 2020 release.
Electrek attended that event, and heard the pronouncements about how the Semi would take over trucking. It would beat diesel trucks in all-in cost per mile, so there’s really no reason a fleet manager should bother buying a diesel truck ever again.
Except, of course, that the Semi has not been available. Despite a whole bleacher full of fleet managers being invited to that event for dealmaking purposes, the Semi took its sweet time to get to scale.
Tesla did deliver its first Semis in late 2022, late but not so late, and that first batch went to PepsiCo and its subsidiary Frito-Lay. And then… not much happened. We didn’t get official counts, but by looking through recall paperwork, it was clear that Semis were being assembled at a glacial pace, if at all.
Since 2021, Tesla has also said that a dedicated Semi production line was being worked on at its Nevada battery factory. Over the years there has been progress on that line, but it has been quite slow.
Finally, this year, the first truck rolled off the dedicated high-volume line, and Semis have been trickling out to other customers over time (and we finally got to ride in one at ACT Expo last year).
So Tesla’s new event to “rollout” the Semi is a little confusing, given that the truck was already unveiled at an event in 2017, delivered at an event in 2022, and the factory started working in April 2026. We’re not really sure what the purpose is for this event, although the next product might give us more of a hint…
The Roadster might get launched, or might get pushed back… for stock pumping reasons
The Roadster is another continually delayed product. First unveiled in the same event as the Tesla Semi in 2017, it was promised to be the car that gave a “hard-core smack down to gasoline powered cars.” But now in 2026, we still don’t have a definitive idea of when it will be released.
Now, perhaps you’ll say that the Roadster doesn’t fit in this article, since there’s no announced launch in September like the other two products. But there was supposed to be a demo in August, which ended yesterday, and a demo has been announced and pushed back many times prior.
(But even if we do skip the Roadster, we could throw in FSD being able to avoid potholes as a planned product upgrade, which was first announced in 2019, and which Musk said this week is “coming soon”)
But more importantly, another recent statement from a former Tesla president could shine some light on the real reason for all these events: that the Roadster delays have all been about bringing Tesla and SpaceX closer together.
The connection is particularly clear in the case of the Roadster, which Musk said early on would be available with a “SpaceX package” to increase performance further, which Musk said would be demonstrated by “the end of next year” in 2019 (hmm, where have I heard that phrase before…).
Originally, that SpaceX package was marketed as using cold gas thrusters to help performance. This is theoretically possible and could be beneficial, if they were used for lateral thrust or additional downforce and if weight was kept down.
But later Musk started saying nonsense like the car would be able to “hover” or “fly“, which does not actually provide a performance benefit (nobody is ever looking for “upforce”). We’ve found other performance patents that would actually be kind of cool, but all the rhetoric has been about SpaceX, flying, rockets and so on.
So why talk about all this stuff if it doesn’t help performance? Well, maybe it’s about a different kind of performance: stock performance.
This is all probably about a merger, which in turn is about getting Musk more money and power
As time has marched on, and especially after SpaceX’s recent IPO, it has become more and more apparent that Musk’s goal is to merge SpaceX and Tesla. This would be beneficial for him personally, because it would allow him to cheat on the goals laid out in his ridiculous stock packages, giving him potentially trillions of dollars in stock value without meeting any of the operational milestones attached to the stock grants that shareholders unwisely voted to adopt.
And if that’s the goal, then there needs to be both a reason for this to happen, and hype that makes investors in one stock want to be involved in the other.
Marketing the Roadster as something that could only be achieved by closer collaboration between the companies offers a possible reason for the merger to happen, and other product unveilings are necessary to give the impression that a company that has only delivered one new product in the last 5 years(and it’s a huge flop) has something going for it in the future.
And the more buzz associated with both companies, the better off Elon Musk will be. The companies won’t necessarily benefit from it – usually in an all-stock merger (as is expected), you want your company to have more value and the other company to have lower value, so you’re getting a better deal; if both go up in value, you’re not really gaining anything. But Musk benefits from higher market caps, because that’s what triggers his stock awards.
The higher the market cap, the more stock he gets personally, and the more every other shareholder’s stake is diluted in order to pay out the worst and most overpaid employee at either company (or any company, for that matter).
Top comment by Dan B
Ok. Someone please help me understand this. Yesterday on the 405 Freeway around the Culver City area, I once again came upon (passed actually) a very distinct gold Tesla Cybercab. I've seen these around this same area several times over the past few months. However, yesterday was the first time I was going the same direction and got a full view as I passed it next to me. First, it had a Texas plate. Second, it was gold with those full wheel discs. Third, it was certainly a Tesla product. But here's what got me. There was a guy clearly in the "drivers seat" AND he had a steering wheel in front of him.
So are they also making these with the wheels and pedals along with the ones without them?
It would be one thing if that dilution came only from the pockets of shareholders who voted against their own interests. But due to the size of each company and Musk’s questionable finagling to get SpaceX added to the Nasdaq 100, a lot of retirement account holders who may not know they have Tesla or SpaceX exposure will have some of their accounts drained away and put into the pockets of someone who has more than enough money and is actively using it to make the world worse.
So, think about this overarching goal when you witness these product announcements this month (or “soon” after). One product isn’t capable of doing the things it’s built and marketed for (and represents a betrayal to customers who purchased software on a promise), one product has already been out for years and the event is just for glitz and glam, and one product has continually been pushed back with little to show except continued promises of SpaceX collaboration.
But all three of them do still serve a purpose: allowing Musk to take more of your money for himself.

title: Tracking the fatal Tesla Autopilot and FSD crashes hidden in its data
content:
Tesla reports its Autopilot and “Full Self-Driving” crashes to the federal government, as it’s required to — and then blacks out almost everything in those reports, so the public never learns what happened in those crashes. Tesla always end up blaming the driver.
We’re matching those redacted reports, one by one, to real fatal crashes that were covered in the news as ordinary accidents. This is a running investigation, and we’ll add each crash we confirm to this page. You can view this as an investigative hub keeping track of our ongoing investigation.
What the data shows
Under a 2021 NHTSA Standing General Order (SGO), automakers must report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone was hurt, killed, or a vehicle was towed. Tesla accounts for roughly 85% of the entire industry’s reports — nearly 4,000 crashes — and the count climbs every year.
We believe that between FSD and Autopilot, Tesla has more mileage on ADAS than any other automaker and therefore, it’s not necessarily a problem that it has more crashes, but it’s nonetheless worrying that crashes are reaching new records each month.
The problem is what Tesla does to those reports. On virtually all of them, it redacts the crash narrative, the software version, and the field for whether the road was within the system’s approved operating area — all as “confidential business information.” It has blacked out the narrative on 99.9% of its reports every single year since 2019.
Almost no other automaker does this. GM, Ford, Honda, and Toyota redact essentially none of their narratives. Tesla is the only high-volume reporter that hides everything.
How we’re doing this
The reports do leave a handful of fields unredacted: city, state, month, vehicle, roadway, a pre-crash speed, and an incident time logged in UTC. That’s enough to match many of them to specific, named crashes covered in the local press.
So we do. We convert the UTC timestamp to local time and line it up against the time police gave; we confirm the city, the vehicle, and the fatal outcome; and we check that it’s the only matching crash that month. Where a case checks out, we lay it out in two columns — everything Tesla told the government, and everything the public was told — and we file public-records requests with the investigating agencies for what Tesla won’t release, including whether police received Tesla’s raw telemetry or only Tesla’s own interpretation of it.
The crashes we’ve confirmed so far
Each of these was reported publicly as an ordinary crash, with no mention of Autopilot or FSD — until Tesla’s own redacted NHTSA report revealed the system was engaged.
- Clute, Texas — Steven Alvarez, 23, died when his Model 3 left the road and hit a park pool. Police called it a possible medical episode. Tesla’s data: driver-assist verified engaged at 104 mph — a speed that appears nowhere in the public record.
- Lake Mary, Florida — a 43-year-old man died when his Model 3 sat stopped in a live I-4 lane and a semi rear-ended it. Troopers said they couldn’t explain why the car was stopped. Tesla’s data: driver-assist verified engaged, at 0 mph.
- Mesa, Arizona — weeks later, a near-identical case: another 2020 Model 3, stopped at 0 mph on Loop 202 at 3 a.m., rear-ended, its driver killed. Same signature, driver-assist verified engaged — and Tesla holds the video.
- Batavia, Illinois — Maggie Espinosa, 37, a teacher and mother of five, was killed as a passenger when a Model Y turning left at an intersection struck a pickup. Tesla’s data: driver-assist verified engaged while making the turn — a maneuver that points to “Full Self-Driving.” The case is now under review by the Kane County State’s Attorney’s Office, and Tesla holds the video.
We’ll update this list as we confirm more.
Why this matters
This is not an abstract transparency fight. Tesla is, more aggressively than ever, encouraging owners to treat a Level 2 driver-assistance system as if it were autonomous. It sells the software as “Full Self-Driving,” Elon Musk repeatedly promises unsupervised autonomy is months away, and the marketing invites drivers to trust the car to drive itself.
But legally and technically, it is still Level 2: the human is driving and is responsible at all times. Tesla’s own actions confirm the gap — it has not removed the supervision requirement from consumer FSD, and its robotaxi service remains a handful of closely monitored vehicles. The technology is not what the branding says it is.
That gap is dangerous, because it breeds complacency — drivers who over-trust the system and stop paying attention. And when things don’t go well, Tesla blames the drivers for abusing the system and releases limited redacted data so we don’t even know what happened.
Tesla is pushing owners to believe the car can handle things itself; it is hiding the records that would show how the system actually behaves when things go wrong. The public is asked to trust the marketing while being denied the data.
Electrek’s Take
Tesla is blacking out the single most important fields in a federal safety database — what its car did, which software was running, and whether the car was even supposed to be operating that way — in reports about crashes that killed people. It justifies this by claiming it would “suffer financial harm” if the information became public. In other words, Tesla is telling regulators that the commercial value of its secrecy outweighs the public’s right to know how its cars behave in fatal crashes. That is indefensible.
Top comment by oldgeek
There's a less charitable interpretation of the claim that tesla would suffer financial harm if more of its crash information was made public. Namely that there's something both really bad and actionable hiding in that data, so that the company would both lose sales and face additional liability.
(Not exactly on point, but in litigation when a defendant destroys or refuses to produce required information, jurors are generally allowed to assume that the information would have damaged the defendant's case.)
You can’t use public roads to test software that you admit is “beta” and then keep the public in the dark when it fails, and someone dies.
It is also selective. When the data makes the software look good, or Tesla can present the data in a way that makes its system look good — as in the fatal Katy, Texas crash, where Tesla could point to the driver overriding the system, the details come out. When they don’t, the report is sealed. A company confident in its technology would not need to hide what its cars did when things go wrong while broadcasting it when they go right.
Tesla is already under NHTSA investigation over how it reports these crashes, and its own AI trainers have told Reuters they don’t trust its safety stats. Electrek’s position is simple: Tesla should stop redacting its SGO crash narratives and software versions, and NHTSA should stop accepting the redactions. As long as it keeps them sealed, we’ll keep doing this the hard way — matching the crashes one at a time, and adding them here.

title: China restores 2% lithium-ion battery tax after 11-year exemption - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
China has begun taxing lithium-ion batteries at 2% from Sept. 1, 2026, ending a decade-long exemption; the rate will rise to 4% in September 2027, while emerging technologies such as sodium-ion and solid-state batteries remain temporarily exempt. The tax applies to cells, packs and battery clusters—not complete BESS—and is expected to modestly raise domestic storage costs, while directly exported batteries remain exempt.
Tristan Rayner
01 Sep 2026
Markets & Policy
Batteries
Energy Storage
China ha puesto en marcha una planta solar offshore de 1 GW.
China has begun collecting consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries from Sept. 1, ending an exemption that had been in place for more than a decade and adding a new cost component for domestic battery energy storage products.
The measure is a legacy tax returning to the industry. China added batteries to its consumption tax regime in February 2015 with a statutory rate of 4%, but exempted lithium-ion batteries, lithium primary batteries, nickel-metal hydride batteries, fuel cells, solar cells and vanadium redox flow batteries as part of policies supporting emerging clean-energy industries.
Under a policy issued jointly by the Ministry of Finance, General Administration of Customs and State Taxation Administration in July, lithium-ion batteries, lithium primary batteries, nickel-metal hydride batteries, mercury-free primary batteries and vanadium flow batteries are now taxed at 2% from Sept. 1, 2026, before returning to the statutory 4% rate from Sept. 1, 2027.
The policy retains temporary exemptions through the end of 2028 for sodium-ion batteries, solid-state batteries and fuel cells. Semi-solid batteries do not qualify as solid-state batteries for the exemption, according to clarification issued by the State Taxation Administration on Aug. 27. Tax-exempt products must also comply with applicable national standards and obtain qualifying test reports.
For the stationary storage industry, the tax authority has clarified an important boundary.
Lithium-ion cells and battery packs are taxable, and battery clusters assembled from cells are also regarded as battery products. However, a complete battery energy storage system incorporating electrical equipment, thermal management, fire protection and control systems is classified as complete power equipment and is not subject to another consumption tax. Taxes already paid on battery inputs can also be deducted when those products are used to manufacture another taxable battery product.
The result is therefore not a straightforward 2% increase in the price of an entire BESS.
Shanghai Metals Market (SMM), a research platform, estimated before the final tax clarification that a 2% rate would add around CNY 0.00648/Wh (~USD 0.9643/kWh) at the cell level based on a lithium-ion cell price of CNY 0.324/Wh (~USD 48.21 per kilowatt-hour). SMM said the final impact would depend on where the taxable boundary was set along the cell-to-system chain.
Huatai Securities estimated that, based on an energy-storage battery price of around CNY 0.40/Wh and assuming full cost pass-through, the tax could add approximately CNY 0.008/Wh at 2% and CNY 0.016/Wh at 4%. The brokerage described the overall impact on storage costs as manageable, while noting that stronger suppliers are likely to have greater ability to pass the cost downstream.
Battery manufacturers have already begun adjusting prices.
EVE Energy circulated a customer notice stating that domestic lithium battery products delivered from Sept. 1 would carry an additional 2% consumption-tax cost. Lishen Battery issued a similar notice in August. CATL also raised the listed price of its 314 Ah storage cell on its online marketplace from CNY 0.414/Wh to CNY 0.423/Wh on Aug. 1, although market supply conditions as well as the tax change contributed to recent cell-price increases.
Export costs exempt
Exports are treated differently. Batteries exported directly remain exempt from consumption tax, while eligible tax already paid on purchased batteries can be refunded. This should not be confused with China’s separate VAT export rebate policy: the VAT rebate for battery products was reduced from 9% to 6% in April and will be eliminated from Jan. 1, 2027.
The change fits into a broader withdrawal of tax preferences for mature Chinese clean-energy manufacturing. Solar-cell consumption tax will also begin at 2% in April 2027 before rising to 4% a year later, while VAT export support for solar products has already been removed. The differentiated treatment also gives the policy an industrial-policy dimension. Mature lithium-ion and vanadium-flow technologies are moving back toward normal taxation, while sodium-ion and solid-state batteries retain a temporary 2-4 percentage-point tax advantage. Huatai Securities described the exemptions as a clear policy tilt toward emerging technologies.
In effect, the tax changes could act as another supply-side reform: reducing support for mature capacity while preserving incentives for technologies still moving toward commercialization to guide industry development.
