title: SLB’s $4.1B Kelvion Deal Expands AI Data Center Push
content:
SLB will spend $4.1 billion to acquire thermal management company Kelvion, expanding its data center business into cooling and heat rejection as AI workloads drive higher power densities.
The deal adds heat exchangers, heat rejection equipment and other thermal management technologies to SLB’s engineering, modular manufacturing, offsite construction, power integration and digital capabilities.
SLB said Kelvion will more than double its revenue opportunity per gigawatt of delivered data center capacity. The combined data center business is expected to generate more than $2 billion in revenue in 2026, with SLB targeting $4.5 billion to $5 billion in revenue by 2028.
“It’s less about what SLB sells today and more about what it becomes,” said Alex Cordovil, research director at Dell’Oro Group.
Until now, SLB has been a relatively small data center player focused on prefabricated modular capacity and integrating third party equipment into delivered facilities, Cordovil said.
Related:
Solid-State Transformers Power Next-Gen AI Data Centers
“Kelvion turns SLB into an OEM in one of the fastest growing corners of the thermal chain,” he said.
SLB’s Data Center Solutions business has grown at a compound annual rate of more than 90% from 2024 through 2026. The company expects cumulative delivered capacity to exceed 2 GW by the end of this year.
Kelvion expects 2026 revenue of $2.3 billion to $2.4 billion and adjusted EBITDA of $350 million to $400 million. Its data center business is expected to generate $1.2 billion to $1.3 billion.
Heat Rejection
AI cooling discussions have focused heavily on direct to chip technologies such as cold plates and coolant distribution units. But heat captured at the chip still has to move through the cooling loop and ultimately leave the facility.
Kelvion gives SLB a larger position in that part of the system.
“Most of the attention has gone to cold plates and CDUs, but the segment repricing fastest right now is heat rejection,” Cordovil said.
He pointed to rising rack densities and pressure over data center water consumption as drivers for dry coolers and hybrid or adiabatic systems, areas where Kelvion has established technology.
SLB said modern GPUs are already pushing rack power densities above 100 kW, while some announced chip architectures could approach 1 MW.
Higher densities increase the amount of heat cooling systems must move and reject at the facility level. Kelvion also has technologies for waterless cooling applications, giving SLB additional options in markets where water availability or community opposition limits conventional cooling approaches.
Related:
Trump Targets Foreign Grid Equipment as Data Centers Expand
Integrated Cooling
SLB plans to integrate Kelvion’s thermal technologies into its modular infrastructure rather than treating cooling as a separate system added later.
Management said that would bring thermal management into the design process alongside SLB’s engineering and manufacturing capabilities.
“This creates a more integrated infrastructure architecture with better alignment across performance requirements, configuration choices and deployment timing for customers,” said Gavin Rennick, president of SLB’s New Energy and Industrial business.
SLB pointed to its work as a modular design partner for Nvidia AI factories as an example. Management said Kelvion’s thermal expertise could help optimize cooling as those systems are designed and fabricated.
Cordovil said integration will determine whether the acquisition produces a lasting competitive advantage.
“Durable differentiation sits in system design and controls rather than in individual components,” he said. “So the test is whether SLB can integrate, not whether it can manufacture.”
Kelvion also supplies components to other companies in the thermal management market, potentially leaving SLB competing with companies that buy Kelvion equipment.
Related:
DOE Retreat on Transmission Corridors Tests the Case for Building Ahead
“SLB now sits as both competitor and supplier to parts of the ecosystem,” Cordovil said.
Beyond Cooling
SLB also sees the acquisition as a potential entry point into other parts of the data center infrastructure stack.
CEO Olivier Le Peuch said the company could combine its modular and cooling capabilities with partnerships for behind the meter generation and other power solutions.
SLB also identified potential opportunities involving geothermal and carbon capture.
“The more interesting question is whether cooling is the entry point rather than the destination,” Cordovil said. “SLB’s core competence is energy, and a growing number of data centers are having to generate their own power.”
The company said it sees an opportunity to offer hyperscalers integrated power, cooling and modular infrastructure as operators seek to secure the infrastructure needed for large AI deployments.
Market Expansion
SLB estimates the data center infrastructure market it can address will exceed $150 billion by 2030, excluding IT and silicon.
Dell’Oro uses a narrower definition and expects the data center physical infrastructure market to surpass $80 billion by 2030, Cordovil said.
Kelvion also expands SLB’s geographic reach. SLB has built its data center business primarily in the US, while Kelvion has established operations and customers in Europe, Asia and the Middle East.
Le Peuch said the US will remain the foundation of the business, followed by Europe and then Asia and the Middle East.
Kelvion’s non data center business also gives SLB exposure to thermal management applications in energy and industrial markets, including heat pumps, renewables, carbon capture and processing.
The Deal
SLB will pay about $3.4 billion in cash and assume about $700 million of Kelvion debt. The transaction values Kelvion at about 11 times estimated 2026 adjusted EBITDA before synergies and about 8.5 times after expected synergies.
SLB expects about $120 million in annual EBITDA synergies within three years of closing. About $70 million will come from cost savings, with the remainder expected from revenue opportunities.
Cost savings are expected from supply chain efficiencies, manufacturing optimization, logistics, service centers and G&A. Revenue opportunities will come from expanding Kelvion technologies across SLB’s customer base and into new geographic markets.
The transaction is expected to close in the first half of 2027, subject to regulatory approvals and other customary closing conditions.
SLB expects the combined data center business to generate $700 million to $800 million in adjusted EBITDA in 2028 alongside its $4.5 billion to $5 billion revenue target.
For SLB, the acquisition moves data centers from a modular construction business into a broader infrastructure strategy spanning engineering, thermal management and potentially power.

How AI Is Changing Construction from Blueprint to Build
AI is reshaping the construction lifecycle. At Ai4 2026, AEC leaders shared how firms are applying AI across design, logistics, safety, and operations, while tackling data standards, culture change, and scaling.
AI is moving deeper into the construction lifecycle, from design and planning through site operations and building performance.
At the Ai4 2026 conference, held August 4-6 in Las Vegas, Amit Sinha (TRC Companies), Jeff Miller (Clayco), Patrick Murphy (Coastal Construction), and Shane Snider (Data Center Knowledge) discussed how construction firms are putting AI to work on major projects.

title: Meeting AI Demand: Alternate Power, Design, and Site Strategy
content:
As artificial intelligence accelerates the transformation of industries, it is also reshaping the very infrastructure that supports it. Developers, architects, and engineers are taking bold steps toward the future by designing data centers specifically to meet the immense computational and energy needs of AI-driven workloads.
Driven by the immense power demands of AI, traditional approaches to power, site design, and infrastructure are no longer sufficient to meet AI’s needs. Developers must deliver forward-thinking engineering and architectural solutions to redefine how data centers are planned, powered, and positioned for long-term resilience and growth.
The following article showcases strategies that integrate cutting-edge energy solutions, AI-optimized floor plans, and site-selection methodologies that anticipate future demand.
Strategies to Meet AI’s Energy Demand
Related:
OpenAI’s Proposed IPO: A Trifecta of Opportunities, But Don’t Lock In Yet
Training sophisticated AI models and running inference for systems like ChatGPT require power densities far exceeding typical data center norms. Recognizing the limitations of existing utility infrastructure, developers must consider alternative energy sources to ensure reliable, 24/7 service.
On-site generation systems
can be engineered to scale with AI workloads while providing redundancy and sustainability. To curb the reliance on gas plants and coal-fired plants, many tech companies are considering low-carbon energy sources such as nuclear power. The implementation of small modular reactors (SMRs) can reduce emissions and the demand for water as a coolant. Tech companies have signed new contracts for more than 10 GW of possible new nuclear capacity in the last year, according to
Goldman Sachs
. Data centers can also operate behind the meter by co-locating load and clean energy generation, reducing the need for grid upgrades and fossil-fuel pollution.
“By planning beyond the boundaries of traditional utility service, facilities can meet customers’ needs without being bottlenecked by local grid capacity or reliability issues – a critical differentiator as AI adoption accelerates,” said Chris Hastings, Vanderweil Engineers’ Power Group Managing Principal.
Related:
How Changing AI Workloads Are Redefining Data Center Design
Design Solutions for Supporting Alternative Power Sources
High energy demand, power density, and complex AI workloads are rapidly changing how we design data centers. Optimizing a data center for AI isn’t simply a matter of adding more server capacity. The design, site, and floor plan must handle AI’s high-density computational requirements, with spaces that support the necessary cooling, power distribution, and flexibility for future upgrades.
The history of designing and constructing programmed spaces and site layouts for data centers has changed over the years, and significantly in the past year. Twenty years ago, the ratio of data halls to support space was 50/50. Today, we’re seeing the building size reduced significantly, but the site area remains the same or increases drastically to accommodate cooling equipment and on-site power generation.
These changes are driven by
increasing rack densities
– from 25-30 kW per rack to as much as 600 kW per rack – as well as moving support space, such as utility power supply and power rooms, outside. As building size changes with higher densities, cooling requirements are rising sharply. Having enough cooling equipment on roofs to prevent the facility from overheating becomes infeasible.
Related:
Preparing Enterprise Data Centers for AI Adoption
“The challenges of site and building planning are tied to the mechanical and electrical system design now more than ever,” said Dutch Wickes, Ci Design, Inc., Principal and Global Mission Critical Practice Leader. “All the variables make a Rubik’s Cube look easy! Especially when you throw in on-site power generation, whether it is bridging power or permanent power. The typical rules of thumb are moot.”
Once a potential site is identified, informed decision-making requires a conceptual plan developed with the client, input from mechanical and electrical engineers, and architectural planning. An integrated, on-site power generation and distribution system that harmonizes with the facility’s architecture could ensure not only operational efficiency but also scalability, enabling the end user to expand capacity without redesigning core systems. These innovations align with broader goals of resilience and sustainability, ensuring the facility is future-proofed against both technological and regulatory change.
Strategic Site Selection
Beyond the traditional criteria of connectivity, proximity to users, and
climate risk
, data center locations must be evaluated for their ability to accommodate off-grid power infrastructure, access to alternative fuels, and regulatory environments supportive of innovative energy solutions.
“Utilities significantly impact data center site selection decisions. We’re seeing data centers emerge in more remote locations that have access to less strained grids, but the lack of adequate power interconnection and infrastructure can pose issues,” said Mason McPike, Provident Data Centers’ Executive Director of Vertical Development & Delivery. “Finding a successful data center site starts with building strong relationships between the end user, government entities, utility companies, and the local community.”
Smart site selection ensures that each facility is located where it can deliver maximum value – not only today, but as AI demands grow exponentially in the coming years. Facilities built close to power plants can overcome these issues, but data centers that generate their own off-grid power using technologies such as fuel cells, batteries, renewable energy, and SMRs may be a more sustainable solution for the environment and surrounding communities.
Positioning for the Future
Early collaboration among the end user, developer, architect, and engineer can position a data center project at the forefront of a rapidly evolving industry. By addressing energy constraints head-on, designing for AI’s unique operational needs, and selecting sites that support a bold, off-grid vision, the industry can set a new standard for how data centers can and should evolve.
“The changing market demand allows us to have an adaptive perspective in how we approach data center development,” McPike said. “Everything has to work in tandem, from finding the right site to sourcing power supply and creating an efficient design. We have to rapidly evolve as the online world continues to grow in response to new technologies.”
For data center professionals, these lessons underscore the importance of rethinking traditional assumptions and embracing integrated solutions that bridge power, design, and location strategies. As AI continues to redefine what’s possible, these forward-looking strategies will define the next generation of mission-critical infrastructure.
